}

2.body: The book is organized into parts: Part I: Getting Started — Install V, write your first program, understand project structure. Part II: Common Programming Concepts — Variables, types, functions, control flow, structs, enums, modules, collections, error handling. Part III: Intermediate V — Generics, testing, concurrency, web development, C interop, advanced features, and a final project. Each chapter builds on the previous ones. Code examples are tested in CI — every V code block in this book is compiled and run automatically.
2.breadcrumbs: Introduction » How to use this book
2.title: How to use this book

60.body:
In V, variables are immutable by default. Use mut to make them mutable: fn main() { name := 'V' // name = 'Go' // Error: name is immutable mut count := 0 count = 1 // OK: count is mutable count++ println(count)
}
60.breadcrumbs: Chapter 3: Common Concepts » Variables and Mutability
60.title: Variables and Mutability

61.body:
V has a rich type system: fn main() { // Integers a := 42 // int b := i64(100) // 64-bit integer c := u8(255) // unsigned 8-bit // Floats pi := 3.14 // f64 e := f32(2.71) // 32-bit float // Other types name := 'V' // string is_ok := true // bool letter := `A` // rune (single character) println('${a} ${b} ${c}') println('${pi} ${e}') println('${name} ${is_ok} ${letter}')
}
61.title: Data Types

96.body: V takes a different approach to memory management than many languages. Instead of manual memory management or garbage collection alone, V offers multiple strategies.
96.breadcrumbs: Chapter 4: Ownership and Memory » Chapter 4: Ownership and Memory
96.title: Chapter 4: Ownership and Memory

97.body:
V automatically decides whether to allocate on the stack or heap: fn main() { // Stack-allocated (small, fixed size) x := 42 arr := [1, 2, 3] // Heap-allocated (large, dynamic) mut big := []int{} for i in 0 .. 1000 { big << i } println('${x} ${arr} ${big.len}')
}
97.breadcrumbs: Chapter 4: Ownership and Memory » Stack and Heap
97.title: Stack and Heap

98.body:
V uses a garbage collector by default. You don't need to free memory manually: fn main() { mut names := []string{} for i in 0 .. 100 { names << 'name ${i}' } // Memory is automatically freed when no longer referenced println(names.len)
}
98.breadcrumbs: Chapter 4: Ownership and Memory » Garbage Collection
98.title: Garbage Collection

99.title: Autofree
